summary: A humorous memo published on April 1. It spoofs SONET by proposing to compress its frames into poetry, calling the method SONET Over Novel English Translation (SONNET). It is informational and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A joke note that pretends fast data can be squeezed into poems. It is for fun and not meant to be used.

subtitle: An April 1st spoof: compressing SONET frames into English sonnets

tldr.problem: SONET frames are large (810 bytes for an OC-1), so wouldn't it be clever to compress them?
tldr.mechanism: Encode each SONET OC-1 frame as a 14-line English sonnet, achieving about 50% compression. Each possible payload maps to a sonnet from a catalog. SONNET compression speeds are designated OCh-# where h represents the 50% compression and # is the underlying speed.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st RFC—it is a joke, not a real protocol. SONET still uses its standard encoding.

today: This is an April 1st RFC and is not a real protocol. SONET uses its standard frame format and is not compressed to sonnets. The memo is enjoyed as a humorous commentary on data compression and technical standards documents.

sections.title: The Joke
sections.content:
This RFC is published on April 1st, 1994, and is a humor document. It pretends to offer a compression scheme for SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) frames by converting them to English sonnets. The author, credited as W. Shakespeare from Globe Communications, proposes that SONET's 810-byte OC-1 frames can be mapped to approximately 400-byte (14-line) sonnets for a 50% compression ratio.

The mapping uses a fictional "Cerf catalog" of sonnets—a reference to the catalog of published English sonnets to 1950. Each of the 2^704 possible SONET payloads is said to have a matching sonnet.
sections.plainLanguage: Pretend we could turn data into poems to make it smaller. It is April 1st, so this is just for laughs.

sections.title: How SONNET Would Work (Joking)
sections.content:
The proposal is simple in concept: replace the SONET OC-1 frame with a sonnet at the sending end, and convert it back to SONET at the receiving end. For example, SONET frame 12 becomes the opening lines of Shakespeare's Sonnet 29: "When do I count the clock that tells the time / And see the brave day sunk in hideous night..."

For higher rates like OC-3, frames can be interleaved or concatenated. Interleaved frames would have interleaved sonnets. Concatenated frames (OC-3c) would have sonnets placed one after another in larger blocks.

The RFC notes that concatenated transmission "makes clear why data communications experts consider concatenated SONET more efficient and esthetically pleasing"—a joke implying sonnets are more enjoyable to read than binary data.
sections.plainLanguage: Just say which sonnet you want, and the receiver looks it up. If you need faster speed, use multiple sonnets stuck together.

sections.title: Timing Considerations
sections.content: The RFC mentions one "critical" concern: "If SONET frames or converted sonnets shift in time, the SONET pointers, or worse, poetic meter, may suffer." This is a tongue-in-cheek warning that timing precision is essential, playing on the idea that both SONET synchronization and the rhythmic meter of sonnets require exact alignment.
sections.plainLanguage: If the timing gets messed up, the data might break, and the poem might not rhyme.

references.text: Cerf, B., "A Catalog of All Published English Sonnets to 1950", Random House, 1953.
